original_value: Global land surface temperature (LST) data derived from satellite-based infrared radiance measurements are highly valuable for various applications in climate research. While in situ validation of satellite LST data sets is a challenging task, it is needed to obtain quantitative information on their accuracy. In the standardised approach to multi-sensor validation presented here for the first time, LST data sets obtained with state-of-the-art retrieval algorithms from several sensors (AATSR, GOES, MODIS, and SEVIRI) are matched spatially and temporally with multiple years of in situ data from globally distributed stations representing various land cover types in a consistent manner. Commonality of treatment is essential for the approach: all satellite data sets are projected to the same spatial grid, and transformed into a common harmonized format, thereby allowing comparison with in situ data to be undertaken with the same methodology and data processing. The large data base of standardised satellite LST provided by the European Space Agency’s GlobTemperature project makes previously difficult to perform LST studies and applications more feasible and easier to implement. The satellite data sets are validated over either three or ten years, depending on data availability. Average accuracies over the whole time span are generally within ±2.0 K during night, and within ± 4.0 K during day. Time series analyses over individual stations reveal seasonal cycles. They stem, depending on the station, from surface anisotropy, topography, or heterogeneous land cover. The results demonstrate the maturity of the LST products, but also highlight the need to carefully consider their temporal and spatial properties when using them for scientific purposes.

result.paraphrase: Satellite-derived global land surface temperature (LST) measurements from infrared radiance are highly valuable for climate research. Although validating satellite LST data sets in situ is challenging, it is necessary to quantify their accuracy. This paper presents, for the first time, a standardized multi-sensor validation approach in which LST products from state-of-the-art retrieval algorithms on AATSR, GOES, MODIS, and SEVIRI are matched spatially and temporally with multiple years of in situ observations from globally distributed stations covering various land-cover types in a consistent way. The method relies on common treatment of all data: each satellite data set is projected onto the same spatial grid and converted to a shared harmonized format, enabling comparison with in situ data using the same methodology and processing. ESA’s GlobTemperature project provides a large standardized satellite LST database that makes studies and applications that were previously difficult to carry out more practical and easier to implement. Depending on data availability, the satellite data sets are validated over either three or ten years. Mean accuracies across the full period are generally within ±2.0 K at night and within ±4.0 K during the day. Station-based time series analyses show seasonal cycles, which arise depending on the station from surface anisotropy, topography, or heterogeneous land cover. The findings show that the LST products are mature, while also emphasizing the need to account carefully for their temporal and spatial characteristics in scientific use.
